title: Can AI really teach your kids?
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham recaps her WorkLife podcast conversation with Leah Belsky, who runs education at OpenAI and previously helped lead Coursera. She expected a debate about AI replacing teachers and instead got a messier discussion of what learning actually is. The long-sought dream of an AI tutor modeled on Bloom's two-sigma finding is further away than Belsky first thought, because tutoring is about noticing, accountability, and emotional presence rather than answering questions well. Graham distills three takeaways: absorbing information is not learning, an AI tutor needs a human in the loop, and students are using AI less to cheat than to build things nobody gave them permission to build. She argues the skill worth teaching is going from noticing a problem to building a prototype. The piece ends by replacing "will AI ruin learning" with a better question about what we want humans to be able to do when intelligence is abundant.
points: Chat can personalize an answer but cannot yet make a student want to learn or sit with them through the struggle, which is what makes tutoring work.
Having AI do low-order learning for kids instead of with them removes the exact friction that builds skill, even when it feels like learning.
Belsky does not expect AI to replace human teachers, because school is a container for motivation, accountability, and the sense that someone sees you.
The more interesting student story is not cheating but building: drug repurposing research, an accessible Wordle, and a food-recovery club project.
The skill worth teaching is moving from noticing a problem to building a prototype, not prompting a chatbot.
quotes: Chat can give you a beautifully personalized answer. It cannot yet make you want to learn, or sit with you while you cry over long division.
Information absorption is not learning, and that difference is the whole ballgame.

But Leah was just as clear about the flip side: if her other kid takes a photo of his long-division homework and Chat solves it for him, it can feel like learning. It is not. It’s outsourcing the exact friction that builds the skill.
School is really a container for exactly those things: structure, community, a reason to show up.

That’s a much more useful and honest way to think about “what is school for?” in an AI world than either extreme — it’s not “school is obsolete” or “AI changes nothing,” it’s “AI can’t do the human part, so the human part is now the whole point.
Leah’s read, and I think she’s right, is: the skill worth teaching isn’t “how to prompt a chatbot.” It’s “how to go from noticing a problem to building a prototype.
not “will AI ruin learning?” but “what do we actually want humans to be able to do in a world where intelligence is infinitely accessible?
